<reason>Side A won decisively by separating offset quality from offset quantity and exposing the flawed incentive structure of Side B's case. Side A showed that because the motion regulates a voluntary marketing label rather than mandating operational cuts, hard-to-abate sectors like aviation and cement—where internal decarbonization is currently technologically unviable—will simply abandon "net-zero" pledges rather than spend billions on uncredited philanthropy. Side B's concessions that the policy is not an operational mandate and that the math of ton-for-ton permanent removal is accurate allowed Side A to prove that a quantity cap trades real climate finance and physical carbon removal for merely silencing corporate press releases.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [A4.4]-[A4.5], Side A dismantled Side B's argument in [B4.2] (where B conceded "the math is correct" on ton-for-ton permanent removal but worried a firm might expand to emit two tons) by showing that under strict quality rules an expanding firm must permanently remove two tons, whereas if it exits the voluntary claim as Side B welcomed, it still emits the two tons while removing zero.</best_rebuttal>
